queue.tree_name: The Centenary Trees of Parque de la Misericordia
queue.recognise: Look for the tall palm at the centre of the walled garden; sequoias, magnolias and a bald cypress stand among the other specimens around it.
queue.story:
More than forty species of tree grow inside the walls of a Bilbao almshouse. The Santa y Real Casa de Misericordia moved to this site in Indautxu in 1872 and laid a romantic-style garden out around itself, and two sources describe what stands there now in the same terms: Spanish Wikipedia counts over forty different species and calls them arboles centenarios, and a Bilbao visitor guide says plainly that these are trees with more than a century of life behind them.

queue.tree_name: The Huff Creek Road White Pine
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 47.9 metres by the register, on a trunk 3.96 metres round. It stands east of Forest Road 2454, Huff Creek Road, visible from the road.
queue.story:
The Wisconsin DNR champion register measured this eastern white pine at 157 feet, 47.9 metres, and you can see it from a gravel road in the Nicolet National Forest. It stands east of Forest Road 2454, Huff Creek Road, with a trunk 3.96 metres round and a crown about 16 metres one way and 15 the other.

That height is the reason to make the drive. The tallest white pine on our Chicago page, the champion of the Cook County forest preserves, is 29.3 metres. This one is more than 18 metres taller, on a trunk well over a metre thicker. Its crown is narrow for that height, barely a third as wide as the tree is tall.

queue.tree_name: The Plane Trees of Jardines de Albia
queue.recognise: The tall plane trees clustered around the 1892 Antonio Trueba statue, right in the middle of the small square.
queue.story:
A photograph from the 1940s shows these plane trees already standing clear of the five-storey buildings around them. They still do. Jardines de Albia is barely 4,500 square metres, one block of green in Bilbao's Abando district, and the trees are what the Bilbao daily Deia reached for in 2023 when it called the square almost unchanged: grandes plataneros, more than a hundred years old, grown to the height of the facades that enclose them.

queue.tree_name: The Great Plane of Brunswick Square
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the information board beside it and by its size, the one very large plane in a small square. It stands in Brunswick Square Gardens in Bloomsbury, with the Foundling Museum on the far side.
queue.story: This plane was planted for orphans. Brunswick Square Gardens was laid out in 1796 as green space for the children of the Foundling Hospital, and this tree is reckoned to date from that laying out, which makes it around 230 years old. Only the planes of Berkeley Square, put in seven years earlier, are commonly held to be older among the planes of central London. It has stood through everything Bloomsbury became, the Hospital selling up and moving out of London in the 1920s, its buildings coming down, the square rebuilt around the gap, the Blitz, and the concrete decks of the Brunswick Centre arriving to the west in the 1970s. The institution it was planted to shade is gone. The tree is not. I

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the single trunk, 6.43 metres round and 22 metres tall, the sixth thickest tree recorded in Berlin. It stands on the north shore of the Lietzensee, about 170 metres along the path from the wingnut.
queue.story:
This plane added 43 centimetres to its waistline in ten years. Measured at chest height it went from 6.00 metres in 2015 to 6.43 metres in 2025, which by circumference makes it the sixth thickest tree on record anywhere in Berlin. A laser measurement in 2025 put its height at 22 metres.

The date usually given for its planting is 1807, an estimate rather than a ring count. That would make it a sapling in an occupied city, the year after Napoleon's army marched through the Brandenburg Gate and took the Quadriga off the top of it to Paris.
